sections.content: The syllabus spans vectors and geometry in 3D, vector-valued functions, partial derivatives and chain rules, directional derivatives and gradients, optimization with Lagrange multipliers, double/triple integrals in various coordinate systems, line and surface integrals, and the three major integral theorems.
sections.teaching:
Teaching quality is the most variable factor. Official course outlines state the course follows lecture notes, with the textbook as supplementary practice . However, student feedback reveals stark contrasts between instructors.

One detailed review of a past instructor (Jimmy) describes him as energetic and approachable, sometimes bringing props and making jokes, but also prone to scheduling 3-hour make-up lectures and holding rigid expectations for how certain problems (like tangent planes) must be written . Another review of a different instructor (Zhang Hai) was highly critical of the lecture logic, though the student ultimately self-studied and scored well . The practical takeaway: do not assume teaching style or effectiveness is uniform. Check the specific instructor's recent reviews before enrolling.
sections.grading: The assessment breakdown shifts between semesters, and the letter-grade philosophy has changed over time.
sections.workload: The workload is moderate to heavy, concentrated in problem-solving rather than written assignments. Homework is entirely on WeBWork, typically worth only 10–16%, and late submissions are not accepted . The official advice is not to take it lightly because it prepares you for exams .

sections.content: A solid, well-structured foundation: limits and continuity in R^n, partial derivatives, gradient and chain rule, directional derivatives, constrained optimization with Lagrange multipliers, double/triple integrals with polar, cylindrical and spherical coordinates, vector fields, line integrals, and Green's, Stokes' and the Divergence theorems. The content builds logically from single-variable calculus (1014) , some vector-calculus theorems feel abstract until you see applied examples.

Here is the weirdest part of the course.

Prof. Ho does NOT give any material (like lecture notes) BEFORE lectures. He only updates his notes online few hours after the lectures.

He does NOT give any past paper.

His choice of focus in classes are also kinda different from that of other profs. And then he skipped the formal proofs of many things, claiming that they require deeper knowledge in more advanced courses.

Nonetheless, he is actually able to explain the concepts kinda clearly during lectures.......

For instance, bro spent like 5-6 lectures on double integral, triple integral, cylindrical/spherical cordinates system, but they DID NOT appear on the exam at all.......................................

Since the question type is so different from textbook/past papers u can find online, drilling them are not too useful, and I literally could not find any material that looks similar to his exams. Therefore, if you are the type of person who needs to drill a lot to get good grade, good luck....

sections.content: The amount of content covered in this course is absolutely insane. We’re expected to master an entire textbook plus dozens of extra research papers and advanced topics in just one semester. It feels like two or three graduate-level courses squeezed into one. Very little time is given to actually digest anything before moving on to the next overload of material.
sections.teaching: The teaching simply cannot keep up with the ridiculous volume and difficulty of the material. Lectures rush through extremely complex concepts at breakneck speed, with almost no time for questions or clarification. Students who don’t already have a strong background in the subject are basically left behind from week 2 onward.
sections.grading: Grading is brutally strict for a course with this much content and this level of difficulty. Exams cover an enormous scope of material, include very tricky questions, and leave almost no room for partial credit. The expectations are completely out of touch with how overloaded the syllabus is.
sections.workload: The workload is probably the heaviest I’ve ever experienced in my university life. Weekly problem sets that take 2–3hours, hundreds of pages of dense readings, multiple long projects, plus preparing for exams that test everything—it’s physically and mentally unsustainable. Most students are perpetually behind and completely burned out.

sections.workload:
The compulsory workload is very low, you do all questions and revise all lecture notes at once is already able to support your exam grade.

However, if you want to achieve a more comfortable grade range (like not falling in C range), your workload will become to do some "HHM reverse-engineering stuffs".

I don't know who is HHM before start of semester, and don't know about his questioning style, so I'm cooked up with C- even I'm burned out after studing.

First, his question-making mindset is making the question as tedious as possible. In normal mul-cal course, theorems like multi chain rule, lagrange multiplier, green/stoke/divergence theorem can significantly reduce calculating workload and help you understand the math/physical meaning of the context. However, he doesn't allow to use any of these theorems above. Instead, he requires you to integrate 4 surface integrals in a same question and directly evaluating a line integral. Since the marks is loose, I advise you use all your power to calculate the required unknown first (like constant k in Q1), ensure the first part is completely correct so that you can write down all steps in next part to obtin most marks. Don't waste your time to evaluating answer out if your time is running out.

Secondly, you need to prepare a dictionary by yourself to somewhat "translate" the wording itself. He uses redundant and useless wording which make the purpose of question become unclear. Here is some examples:
→ Explicit Value --> Evaluate the exact answer
→ Cannot use theorem involving double/triple integral --> Cannot use green and stokes theorem, evaluate line integral directly
→ "I prove this statement" and "... is differentiable at..." --> Prove differentiability write all the stuff you memorized about lecture notes 13 (also can use eplison-delta function in final exam)
→ Triple integral=Double integral(s) --> Prove stokes theorem, write down all things you memorized in lecture notes 35
These phrases can let you having a clear direction for what to do, at least obtaining some step marks. Also, please memorize the wordings apeared in the mid term and write down into dictionary, since HHM asking style is consistent. (but don't revise the question, they won't reappear in final)

Thirdly, HHM won't mention prove questions in either lecture or his lecture notes. Since this course is not mathematical analysis, I suggest you to use AI to generate a prove, then memorize by yourself and write all out in the exam.

Make sure able to break down contents in all computational question and you will slightly above mean.

I used the playlist from Dr. Trefor to study: https://youtube.com/playlist?list=PLHXZ9OQGMqxfW0GMqeUE1bLKaYor6kbHa&si=bYg1ZmkeuG5CZ2jf

I suggest starting early and be clear about the intuition, it’s not easy to cram and be comfortable with the theories (as the whole vector calculus from line integrals to surface integrals, greens theorem to stokes theorem and divergence theorem), it’s just keeping on generalising the same thing, it takes some time to hone the intuition to be comfy with the similarities and differences (not really trivial if you do not have I phy O background (especially EM)). BTW, HHM skipped stokes theorem and divergence flux form of greens theorem (it is useful tho), but included divergence theorem and curl form of greens theorem.

Update: some other comments said graphing is important. To me, it’s important for building the intuition and important for problem solving for materials only after mid term. It’s critical for setting bounds for double and triple integrals. In this part, I think HHM’s notes are great as the steps are clearly outlined. Next, for vector calculus, graphing is also critical but in another sense, we have to be very intuitive with some common graphs like cones and cylinders and spheres (be sure to know their forms in different coordinate systems) The graphs need to capture the essence, but not overly accurate or detailed (there’s no way you draw a whole vector field anyways)

If you have no prior knowledge, it does feel a lot and the pace is fast, but when you finally understand it, you will feel like it’s actually not a lot to be covered, I’d say it’s the total opposite of comp 2711(H) which touches the surface of a lot of things, here, there’s only one focus (which is fundamental theorem of calculus), but it’s deep and elegant.
I’d say for non math or physics majors like data science, MAEC QFIN, this course may be a bit too heavy, but it’s really fruitful to lay a solid foundation of later applied math like (ordinary & partial) differential equations (slope fields as vector fields)

What’s important but not included and suggested to study on your own:
1. Stokes theorem
2. Flux form of greens theorem
3. Gradient descent (arguably the most important application but is not mentioned)
4, Jacobian matrix (the idea is there for change in coordinate system but didn’t talk about Jacobian)
5. Change of variable (because Jacobian is not formally taught)

Overall: as HHM’s teaching approach is to focus on solving problems (but asking proofs and much harder problems in the exam…), the pacing didn’t allow him to actually cover enough content for the course, but it lays a solid foundation as it’s our first touch on multivariable and spatial concepts. (In fact, math 2023 = math 2050 and math 2060 in CU, and cal III + cal IV in overseas uni, covering 2 courses in one sem isn’t easy)

Lastly, here is my final reminder, which I make it for myself to not forget the basic formulae: https://drive.google.com/file/d/1QEs-rF-ij7VkBoYlOKtf1tCQ6i8OW3Ho/view?usp=drivesdk

And here’s another final notes made by two very smart people, one study IRE PMA and another study physics: https://drive.google.com/file/d/1OfqyOTPBEuGaIZt-wktUCyEr_mHu-xsV/view?usp=drivesdk
sections.teaching:
I cannot actually say his teaching is bad, but reading his notes is good enough. I like his notes except the watermark, very detailed. Unpopular opinion: his notes is better than FF’s. As I read more and more, HHM really takes the L1 approach in 1013 and 1014 here and make things quite formal (no epsilon delta la but the idea is there) (like open connected region).
However, his teaching has almost no resemblance to the final exam questions as the questions types are totally different in terms of the theorems and tricks involved and the difficulty. The most typical discrepancy is that when you do the examples, you are working with some given formulae and you can manipulate them easily. However, in the exam, the formulae given are more abstract and it’s more like a description of the function with certain conditions rather than some actual functions and formulae, which takes some time to adapt to, but it’s hard to find these questions cuz HHM style is so unique.

Nonetheless, because of his notes and his clear explanation (although I went to first 2 classes only and decided to self study), also because of his warm reminders and encouragement in emails, I kinda like him and he’s really responsible and takes everything seriously. Would be an A if he covers more theoretical knowledge. But his notes are definitely S tier.

Grading is good in the sense that it’s better than absolute grading. Normally, 65-70 is mean and C+, and then 85 is A-, 90 is A. Here, 53 is mean and is B-, 73 is A- and a few marks more will be A, HHM is much nicer if you know how to survive.

Next, I will tell you what to do to survive HHM exams. Notice that you have to face monsters from 1023,1024, IRE PMA 1013/4 L1, but I’m from regular 1013 and 1014, so I’m on your side. Follow along.

TLDR: For mid term. First 4 Qs are normal, so just get them correct and you’ll be above 1sd, then try to write something for Q5 even though it’s complete nonsense to get a few points.

TLDR: Final exam (here is the survival guide as the final exam is crazy): just do all the computational questions and make sure you don’t get anything wrong. Then, you will be more than 1sd, and then write a few words for the proof questions and get some partials to set your score higher.

Mid term detail: Basically, the last question (see attachment) https://drive.google.com/file/d/1Nb4ZwjRMXMm65oejrTTwMiyzDBHwhvwV/view?usp=drivesdk is real analysis. We never expected that this will happen in mid term because a standard multivariable calculus course is supposed to be computational and intuitive (this course is not tailored for math major) so for non-math majors or weak math majors, 15 marks are gone. Also, I think for differential multivariable calculus, Lagrange multiplier is probably the most useful tool but he didn’t test anything on it. Conversely, he deliberately made a question that prohibited us from using Lagrange multiplier. Despite the beauty of the question, I think it’s not so meaningful considering the purpose of this course. However, I think he’s improved, as the computation isn’t really hard despite the first question with all unknowns, and the final answers are all really nice numbers like 1, -1, 2. Anyway, as a weak math major myself, I’m not ready to do multivariable analysis and I was caught off guard. For non-math majors, you probably would hate him. I think math 2023 deserves an L1 like 1013 and 1014, and HHM should instruct 2023 L1, so we are ready to enter into the “vectorial perspective” with him.

Note: mid term score is out 5 days after the mt (HHM efficiency), the mean is 42.1/73, with sd 14.89 (also out of 73), 2 people got 73/73 (compared to 14 people last year means that this year he became crazier, but the mean didn’t drop by too much) Q1-4 are computational, getting them all correct will give you 58 marks (mean + 1sd is 56.99), It translates to a very safe A range (A- or A depends on final exam)

He posted an announcement saying that doing Webwork will be useful for finals. But…

Final details: First, doing webwork is absolutely useless. Second, doing other professors’ papers is also useless. The exam paper goes like this: first 4 questions (15 marks, 16 marks, 20 marks, 12 marks) are calculation questions (first one about triple integral, second one about conservative vector field, 3rd one about scalar surface integrals, 4th one about 2D flux) and the last 2 questions (16 marks, 16 marks) are proof based (one about differentiability but harder than mid term (yeah… didn’t expect to see it again after mid term and I gave up) and one about 3D flux). Basically, if you don’t study analysis or the proofs of the theorems (some are not even included in the lecture notes), you won’t get the last questions at all. So, only 4 questions are doable out of 6 for normal people. However, it took me a long time to actually write something even for those questions. It goes like this: First, the questions are long and with complicated notations, I suggest translating those clauses into simpler words for context before you actually start doing the questions. Next, you have to use specific methods as he writes a complete guide to what the answers should look like (in some extent it’s good cuz you can check whether your answer is in a good form and the questions have nice answers) However, the conditions he gave are mostly puzzling and you won’t be able to get insights from them immediately until you proceed to a certain step (and then you will directly apply the results given) (for example, you have to calculate something in exact value, but let’s say you write a full page and end up with the answer xyz”, and then somehow he has told you that x = 0, so the whole thing is 0), so the suitable mental model is you don’t stare at the question for too long, you try to solve the question, it’s like you try to swim. Then, to a point, you will suddenly see a rock and you can step on it, and then you will arrive at the coast.
Also, the whole exam is about manipulating the integrand, seeing what can be substituted after some parametrisation, and the computations are heavy. Also, there are a lot of theorems which makes computation easy or is useful when applied to other fields like physics, data science, economics, etc. and that is actually the whole point of learning those theorems and taking this course. However, in his exam, he doesn’t allow you to use those theorems, like greens theorem (flux form, he didn’t teach but he made a question that could be solved immediately using it but he doesn’t allow us to use it). Also, I got confused by his wording in last Q, I knew it was about divergence theorem and I memorised the whole proof, but he said we cannot use the theorem, so I was stuck and left it blank. However, my friends who managed to solve the problem said that it’s basically proving the divergence theorem with the specific functions given, so I lost all the scores just because I don’t understand what he’s asking, but not because I don’t know the knowledge, that’s really saddening…..

4 days after the exam, grade is out, and the partial credits given are much more lenient than expected, I got about 7 marks more than my expectation, which significantly led to a higher grade. So, for the proof questions, don’t try to solve it, try to write down whatever you know about it, especially the definitions, and write as many as you can without going too deep is also enough for a decent score. (Cuz his proofs are decently short, so maybe you’re halfway there just by writing down everything you know)

Update: In Q5, I literally just wrote “I prove this statement.” and nothing else, and got 1 mark.
Next, the grading of Q5,6 is super lenient and I only managed to write a few lines in Q6 and I got 5 marks/ 16 marks, all my friends got more than me despite not being able to finish the proof. It’s not hard to get half of the marks (I would have gotten more than half in Q6 if I ignored everything and went on to prove divergence theorem) So just write whatever you can.
The grading is exceptionally decent, despite not being able to do mid term Q5 (3/15), final Q5 (1/16), final Q6 (5/16), I still managed to get A range (I expected B+ after the exam). For those proofs, being able to do one of them fully will give you an A+. If you study hard not by doing a lot of questions, but by really understanding everything, you definitely don’t need to be smart to be in A range.

Ultimately, what’s not tested (ironically the most important ones):  
1. Lagrange multiplier (prohibited us from using (although for that question he made some tricks to make the boundary have a constant value so Lagrange becomes totally useless)
2. Greens theorem (prohibited us from using it again, …)

4. Integrals in polar coordinates and spherical coordinates
5. Chain rule

Comment: you see, he doesn’t test the important things, and takes a rather abstract pure math approach. Also, for each question, he restricts your answer in a particular format or else you will get 0 marks, I don’t think that’s good for maths as it hinders creativity. Also, there are a lot of things in the syllabus that are not tested, but are meant to solve real world problems or at least make computations easier (Lagrange, greens, divergence) and he forced you to do the most annoying calculations and do proofs that are arguably out of syllabus, I really don’t see the point at all.

What’s heavily tested (ie HHM style):
1. Both exams Q5: Differentiability (proofs) (both in mid term and finals, from lecture notes 13)
2. Q3, 4: manipulating integrands in vector calculus with a strange use of his conditions (more like a riddle game, not hinted by any lecture notes nor exercise you can get  from… but don’t worry, you have found something previous years people (including me) never have (not even Math society has this), which is HHM’s paper)
3. Heavy computations…: Q2 is an ugly vector field…, Q3 is splitting into 2 line integrals with no numbers, Q4 is compute surface integrals for 4 times… just a bunch of algebraic manipulations with finally some nice answers
4. Short hands (I think are quite important): dS = lgradientldA (for scalar surface integrals), nds = <dy, -dx> (for flux across curve)

What’s somehow tested from his lecture notes but I don’t see importance in:
1. Q3: Last page of lecture note 34, this immediately makes some surfaces have surface integral 0 (idk how it’s useful other than in HHM paper…)
2. Q4a: last page from lecture note 7, the parametrisation looks something like a kings theorem in integrals

Final note: he kept emphasising that final exam is cumulative, but it’s a bluff. As a student who has had the opportunity to learn from Professor Ho, I must commend their teaching approach. The notes provided by Professor Ho were comprehensive and left no stone unturned. They covered all the necessary concepts, theories, and examples, making it easier for us to grasp the subject matter. The PowerPoint presentations were visually appealing and organized, enhancing our learning experience during lectures.

However, I must admit that I encountered some challenges when it came to the exam paper. To my surprise, the questions on the exam were significantly more difficult than what we had encountered in the notes and presentations. It felt like the exam was testing us on concepts that were not adequately covered or explored in class.

sections.teaching:
Hai Zhang teaches well and seems to care about your understanding, even in online mode. He often teaches some of the intuitive ideas and proofs behind the concepts we use, even if it's not strictly required. The lectures are usually fairly interesting, which is no accident as I see he prepares the content very well.

In online teaching, he is good at keeping up with the chat and responds to questions quickly. He is also very approachable by email (more so than the TA I got).

However, his accent is quite hard to understand at times. He also goes too fast sometimes, and I have to review the lecture notes immediately after class to understand something.

I did read that others found him too quiet at times, but it's not a problem in online teaching it seems.

The tutorials are a good place to review concepts taught a week ago and ask questions on anything unclear. I found they usually are about a week behind the lectures in terms of content, which is good as you will have somewhat digested the content before reviewing it.

- Pretty essential if you intend to further pursue a major in math. Really advise taking Math 2011/2023 right after you finishing 1014.

- Advantage over 2011 (which is commonly thought to be easier) is that, you could learn about the calculations and theorems in greater detail: Divergence theorem and Stokes' Theorem are not taught in 2011 - they provide you with convenient methods to transform flux integrals into forms that are much easier to evaluate.

sections.teaching:
Although sometimes with local accents and explanations only in Chinese, Jimmy did engage me greatly with body languages, jokes (e.g. about food when discussing forms of 3D surfaces, or "go in one ear and out the other" (左耳入右耳出) in discussing flux) and his enthusiasm.

He would also responsively explain the concepts to you once again if you don't understand them at first - just be proactive and reach him out!

Or if you don't prefer always attending classes early in the morning/ or watching the zoom recordings (like me, sorry Jimmy...), go tutorial exercises! Theorem statements/ examples and exercise solutions are provided and I think they are intelligible enough to students within 1-2 hours of digesting each.

Compared to the (boring, I am sorry) classes I've attended in MATH 1013/14 last year, this math course is definitely much more engaging and meaningful! Kudos to Jimmy :P

Exams were said to be really challenging in the past, particularly in the case for prof. Ip (who usually teaches in spring). However, Jimmy was quite easy-going examwise in the finals and featured relatively simple questions compared to past years' finals.

sections.workload:
Homeworks could be of slight pain, particularly when you are finding the theorems a bit hard to digest well within a limited time. There were 10 (almost weekly) compulsory homeworks on Webwork with 10 questions each; questions featured were of standard type but only 3 attempts were given, so you might need to be quite careful. I spent ~1.5 hours for each piece of the homework for the last few pieces as they could be a bit hard to solve when you're still not yet familiarised with the items taught.

TA provides notes and exercises for each of the topics taught; though those pieces of exercises are optional, I STRONGLY advise anyone taking MATH 2023 to go over them and summarize the strategies required to solve the questions - to get what the theorems or proofs mean.
Spoilers (sorry): there were on average 30-50 questions on each (of the 12) tutorial notes and they usually take a few hours to complete - to get yourself reasonably equipped and perform well in your assessments, some hard work is definitely expected...

There are also optional "exercises for students" made by Jimmy himself, with more challenging questions featured. If you want to get a good grade, at least try going over the suggested (underlined by him) ones as they really do provoke your thoughts rather than being merely "train-up" materials.

After all, this is a 4-credit course so you should expect some workload...

sections.content:
Calculus III
Ch1: Vectors and the geometry of space
Basic vector stuffs, most of them should be covered in MATH1014. Together with some 3D geometry.

Ch2: Vector-valued functions
Parametrisation of curve. Actually I don't know what is going on here when I study this topic.

Ch3: Partial derivatives
Derivatives in 2 or more variables, computation wise is similar to those in single variable calculus. However, there is a big difference in concepts like Differentiability, Continuity, Existence...I still don't know what they are after finishing this course...

Ch4: Application of partial derivatives
Gradient for local max/min/saddle points, Lagrange's Multiplier for max/min in boundary. Finding the absolute max/min. (This should be very useful in many other subjects.)
-----midterm-----
Ch5: Multiple integrals
Double Integral, Triple Integral, Iterated Integral, Integration techniques (spherical coordinate, cylindrical coordinate), curves, surfaces, Change of Variable (Jacobian Determinant)

This chapter is very important as it will be the tool to solve all questions in Ch6.

Ch6: Vector calculus
Vector fields, Curls, Divergence, Conservative Vector Fields, Line Integrals, Surface Integrals, Green's Theorem, Divergence Theorem, Stoke's Theorem

Exciting Chapter, FINALLY I KNOW WHAT I AM DOING FOR THE PAST 5 CHAPTERS. If you have studied PHYS1112 before, then all the ideas of Ch6 will prove so many things that your professor skipped (like path independence, work done along a curve, moment of inertia (Maybe you know this in Ch5)). Since there is so many theorems and different kinds of cases you have to considered (in R^2, R^3, orientations of the curves/surfaces, parametrisation of the region...), this will be the hardest chapter...but still very exciting in learning them. (Maybe it is more applicable and can be visualised easily)

Ch7: Differential forms (For curiosity only, not in final)

Your basics in Math1013 and 1014 will determines how good you are in early chapters. Something you thought is a baby in single variable calculus will become a monster in mulcal :)

sections.content:
The content covers an appropriate breath and depth of both differential and integral calculus with multiple variables.

The first and second week are simply just reviews on the vectors, line equation and plane equations. This is simply a review of material learnt in high school.

The third week to the sixth week, covers mainly the differential calculus portion, which includes partial derivatives, directional derivatives, tangent planes, multivariable functions and Lagrange multipliers.

From then on, was the integral calculus and vector calculus portion. This includes material such as field vectors, line integrals, Green's theorem, Stokes' theorem (not discovered by Stokes') and Divergence theorem.

Overall, the content covered is not overwhelming and would benefit those who would want to pursue a career in engineering, physics or mathematics.
sections.teaching: Professor Ivan Ip is a very good lecturer as not only does he have the enthusiam to teach but he is also quite entertaining, allowing the students to engage in the lessons. I was suprised that he was willing to teach the generalized Stokes' theorem and some suffix notation which is required in tensor calculus. Like myself, those who would want to pursue a career in pure mathematics or theoretical physics, this will most likely spark your interest.

sections.content:
This course is a direct follow-up to content from MATH1014 Calculus II. After reviewing concepts on vectors and equations in three dimensions, the course introduces multivariable functions. Key concepts include:
- Arc-length Parametrization
- Partial Derivatives & Chain Rule
- Directional Derivatives & Gradients
- Tangent Planes, Critical Points
- Lagrange's Multipliers
- Double & Triple Integrals
- (Conservative) Vector Fields & Line Integrals

sections.teaching:
Prof. Fong has prepared a beautiful summary document of lecture content, organized like a short textbook. His lecture slides are written in class, and extremely organized and easy to follow. Every class follows the same format: review, lecturing main concepts, and examples. This format made content easy to learn and understand.

sections.grading:

sections.workload: The only graded homework is weekly WebWork assignments. Problem sets are also given weekly and covered in tutorials, but they are optional. Extra WebWork questions are also provided for students who would like extra review.
